newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel seeks clarity on inflation-Frenkel.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel seeks clarity on inflation-Frenkel.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Monday attributed the decision to hold interest rates steady for August to get a better idea of how inflation is moving.

"We decided to keep rates unchanged this month in a desire to see greater clarity of the picture, especially in view of the fact that recently additional policy measures have been annnounced," Frenkel told Reuters in an interview.
Frenkel referred to last month's changes to the exchange rate regime, which led to a depreciation of about four percent in the shekel, and to an easing of foreign currency controls.
"We will need to see how the markets continue to absorb them and, especially in this context, we will need to examine the implication of these measures on inflation forecasts," he said.

The central bank's decision on Monday to leave its key rate unchanged at an annual 12.7 percent followed a sharp reduction of 1.2 percentage points last month as well as the publishing of June's consumer price index, which rose by a sharp 1.1 percent.
"Our approach in setting interest rates is cast in a medium term perspective rather than influenced by a single monthly index," Frenkel said.
"It is obvious we will need to continue monitoring developments on the inflation front and make assessments on the likelihood that the inflation target set by the govenrment is being met."
The government's 1997 inflation target is 7-10 percent.
Frenkel noted that the capital markets' inflationary expectations, which the central bank closely monitors, have risen recently.

"We will need to verify if this indicates a new trend which will need to be countered...or whether it represents a temporary reaction to the last monthly price index which was higher than initially expected. Much of this dust should settle within the next month," the governor said.

Frenkel said he has urged the government to announce its inflation target for 1998 and for subsequent years to demonstrate a "clear trajectory" and a commitment to reducing inflation to levels prevailing in industrialised countries.

"There is no doubt that the overall economic strategy should include a bold effort to increase competition in the market place, to liberalise the economy and to adopt significant measures for the elimination of foreign exchange controls. This strategy has been adopted by the government and I am looking forward to its early implementation," he said.
Frenkel would not comment directly on the Treasury's recent forecast that the economy will remain sluggish in 1998.

"In can only say that in my judgement the performance of the Israeli economy in the coming years depends heavily on the economic policies that will be in place. It is clear that the large budget deficits and high inflation do not promote sustainable growth," he said.

"It's clear to me that a vigilant effort to stick by the budget deficit reduction law, to stick by the inflation reduction decision will contribute to sustainable growth, especially if accompanied by massive structural changes that enhance competition, that speed up privatisation, that reduce the size of government and thereby lower the tax burden."
